## Setup: packages

Today's main lesson uses dplyr, tidyr, stringr, forcats, and lubridate.
If you installed the full tidyverse, these may already be available.

In the **Console**, check:

~~~r
requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)
requireNamespace("tidyr", quietly = TRUE)
requireNamespace("stringr", quietly = TRUE)
requireNamespace("forcats", quietly = TRUE)
requireNamespace("lubridate", quietly = TRUE)
~~~

Install any package returning `FALSE`, for example:

~~~r
install.packages("lubridate")
~~~

Keep installation commands in the Console. The supplied `library()` calls
belong in the report. Optional practice 5 needs dplyr 1.1.1 or newer:
check `packageVersion("dplyr")` and update if necessary, then restart R.

Replace **Your name** in the starter's author field. Either report format is fine.

## How to work through the lab

At each **Pause and predict**, discuss your answer with a neighbour before
running code. Then run the example and compare the result with your prediction.
The Rmd and Qmd starters contain expandable **Code suggestion** sections with
short syntax reminders and partial examples, not full solutions. Adapt and
complete them in the executable chunks; the suggestions do not run on rendering.

The instructor may select a few pause questions during lab. You do not need to
write a separate essay for each question.

## Core tasks

### 1. Row units and keys

State what one row represents in `patient_lookup` and `marker_wide`.
Use `count(id) |> filter(n > 1)` to check both tables.
Identify the participant appearing only in each table by inspecting the data.

### 2. Join and inspect unmatched participants

> **Pause and predict: first join.** Measurements contain P01, P02, P03, P05.
> Metadata contain P01, P02, P03, P04. With measurements on the left, how many
> rows will remain? Who will have a missing treatment label?

> **Pause again before reversing the join.** A report must include every
> enrolled participant. Which table belongs on the left? Who will now have
> missing measurements? Run the reversed join and check your prediction.

Save `joined_wide` with a `left_join()` of `marker_wide` and `patient_lookup`
by `id`. Compare row counts before and after. Use `anti_join()` in both
directions. Explain the missing arm value. How many rows would an `inner_join()` keep?
If the report instead needs every enrolled participant, which table belongs
on the left? Run that reversed join as `enrollment_report` and inspect it.

### 3. Wide to long

> **Pause and sketch.** Four participants, two measurement columns: how many
> rows will `pivot_longer()` produce? What will one row represent? Sketch P01's
> two rows before running the code.

Reshape `marker_wide` and save `marker_long`. Use
`cols = starts_with("marker_w")`, `names_to = "week"`,
`names_prefix = "marker_w"`, and `values_to = "marker"`.
Then use `mutate(week = as.integer(week))`.
Predict the row count and explain what one row represents now.
Name one analysis or display that benefits from this long format.

### 4. Return to wide

Save `marker_back` using `pivot_wider()` with `id_cols = id`,
`names_from = week`, `values_from = marker`, and `names_prefix = "marker_w"`.
Compare IDs, column names, and values with `marker_wide` after sorting by ID.
Explain why this wide form is convenient for calculating week-4 minus baseline.

### 5. Clean and search text with stringr

> **Pause and compare.** Will `str_trim("  repeat   visit  ")` remove the
> spaces between the two words? Which function would you choose for those spaces?

The documented ID rule is uppercase with no outer spaces. Save `patients_text`
from `raw_patients` using `mutate()`: clean `id` with `str_trim()` and
`str_to_upper()`; clean `arm` and `note` with `str_squish()` and
`str_to_lower()`. Keep the raw table unchanged.
Show the IDs and notes where `str_detect(note, fixed("repeat"))` is true.

### 6. Factor labels and order with forcats

> **Pause and predict.** If Treatment is the first level and you move Control
> first with `fct_relevel()`, does any participant switch treatment groups?
> How is that different from renaming a label with `fct_recode()`?

Save `patients_factor` from `patients_text`. Use `fct_recode()` to map
`control` to `Control` and `treated` to `Treatment`. Then use
`fct_relevel()` to put `Control` first. Print the levels and counts.
Explain which step changes labels and which step changes only their order.

### 7. Parse dates with lubridate

> **Pause and question the result.** R successfully parses `"03/04/2026"`.
> Does that prove the date is correct? What information do you need from the
> source before choosing a parser?

Save `patients_clean` from `patients_factor`. Convert `enrolled` with
`ymd()` into `enrolled_date`. Add `enrolled_year` and `enrolled_month`
using `year()` and `month()`. Inspect the result and check for missing parsed
dates with `filter(is.na(enrolled_date))`.
Explain why `"03/04/2026"` needs a stated month/day or day/month convention.

### 8. Combine the cleaned data

> **Pause before summarizing.** If the result contains an `NA` arm group,
> does that mean the study has a third treatment? What should you inspect?

Save `analysis` by left-joining `marker_long` to the `id`, `arm`, and
`enrolled_date` columns of `patients_clean`. Check the row count.
Keep week 4 and summarize mean marker by arm using Session 6's verbs.
Explain the group with missing arm instead of silently removing it.

## Additional practice

Practices 1–4 reinforce the main lecture. Practices 5–6 correspond to optional
slides and are not prerequisites for completing the core lab.

### Practice 1. Left versus inner

On `marker_long` and `patient_lookup`, compare left and inner joins by ID.
Explain why their row counts differ by two rather than one.

### Practice 2. Spaces inside a note

Compare `str_trim("  repeat   visit  ")` and
`str_squish("  repeat   visit  ")`. Explain which preserves the extra internal spaces.

### Practice 3. A complete factor order

For `factor(c("a", "b", "c", "a"))`, use `fct_relevel()` to set the order
to `c, b, a`. Show the levels and the character values to confirm that
reordering did not relabel observations.

### Practice 4. Three date formats

Use `ymd()`, `mdy()`, and `dmy()` to read `"2026-10-18"`,
`"10/18/2026"`, and `"18/10/2026"`. Show that they represent the same day.

### Practice 5. Optional join detail: relationship check

> **Optional pause: count matches, not just IDs.** One P01 measurement matches
> two different P01 treatment records. How many rows come from that one input
> row? In this lab P01 has two visits: how many P01 rows and total rows will the
> long-table join produce? Is keeping the first metadata row a justified fix?

Only after the optional join slides: the supplied `conflicting_lookup` has two
different arm records for P01. Join `marker_long` to it without a relationship
assertion and inspect the row count. Then request `relationship = "many-to-one"`
and explain the expected error. Use the supplied error-display chunk only for
this deliberate failure.

### Practice 6. Optional window example: previous visit

> **Optional pause.** Why must observations be ordered by week and grouped by
> participant before using `lag()`? What should happen at the first visit?

Only after the optional window slides: arrange `marker_long` by ID/week,
group by ID, and compute `change = marker - lag(marker)`. Ungroup afterward.
Explain the missing first change for each participant.

## Intentional error in optional practice 5

Only the relationship-check chunk uses `error=TRUE` so a deliberately failing
join can appear in the report. The Quarto equivalent is `#| error: true`.
Other analysis errors should stop rendering so you can fix them.

## Exit evidence

Knit/Render your report. Show the join checks, a wide/long round trip, cleaned
text, factor levels, and parsed dates. Explain any missing metadata and verify
that your final row count matches your prediction.
